e.etymology: The Urdu and Persian pronunciation of Arabic duha, the bright light of mid-morning. Ad-Duha, the Morning Hours, is the name of a chapter of the Quran.
A spelling of Isla with a final h. Isla comes from Islay, an island off the west coast of Scotland. Islah is also an Arabic word for reform or setting things right.

assoc.t: Islah, 2016 hit album by rapper Kevin Gates

e.note: The s is silent, as in island; people reading it cold may say IZ-luh.

e.etymology: A French surname and word for russet or red-haired, from Latin russus, red. English speakers know roux best as the cooked flour-and-fat base of gumbo and sauces, a term from the same word.

assoc.t: roux, the flour-and-fat base of gumbo and sauces

e.note: The x is silent; expect some to say ROWKS or to think of the cooking term.

e.etymology: A recent American name with no settled origin. It sits close to the Biblical name Amaziah and to popular names such as Amari and Kamari.
A form of Charissa, built on Greek charis, grace, and used by Edmund Spenser in The Faerie Queene (1590). The C spelling also recalls Latin carissima, dearest.
An English surname meaning son of Neil, from the Irish name Niall. It is also treated as a relative of the Scandinavian Niels and Nils, short forms of Nicholas.

assoc.t: Niles Crane, Frasier's fussy brother on Frasier
Niles, the butler on The Nanny
Niles, towns in Illinois, Michigan and Ohio

e.etymology: The Polish and Dutch spelling of Isaac, from Hebrew Yitzchak, he will laugh. In Genesis, Sarah laughed when told she would bear a son in old age, and the child was named for it.
namesakes: Izaak Walton (author of The Compleat Angler)

e.etymology: From Japanese sakura, the flowering cherry tree and its blossom, the emblem of spring in Japan. It has long been among the most popular girls' names there.

assoc.t: Sakura Haruno, heroine of the Naruto anime
Cardcaptor Sakura, manga and anime heroine
Sakura, fighter in the Street Fighter games
Sakura art pens, maker of Pigma Micron and Gelly Roll

e.etymology: A form of Elijah and Elias, from Hebrew Eliyahu, my God is Yahweh. The spelling Eliah appears in the King James Bible, and Norwegian and Swedish use it beside Elias.
An English spelling of the Irish Niamh, bright or radiant, a princess of the Otherworld in Irish legend. Neve is also the Italian and Portuguese word for snow, from Latin nix.
namesakes: Neve Campbell (actress in Scream and Party of Five)

e.etymology: From Hebrew uri, my light or my fire, from or, light. In the Bible, Uri is the father of Bezalel, the craftsman who built the Tabernacle.

assoc.t: Winter Storm Uri, the 2021 Texas deep freeze

e.etymology: From Sanskrit yuvaraja, joining yuvan, young, and raja, king: the young king, the title of an heir to the throne.
A spelling of Leila or Layla, from Arabic layla, night. The name reached English through 19th-century literature and the Arabic love story of Layla and Majnun.

assoc.t: Layla, the Eric Clapton rock classic, by sound

e.etymology: A spelling of Lia, the Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Leah, from Hebrew Le'ah, the first wife of Jacob in Genesis. This spelling is especially liked in France.
From Persian mehr, kindness or affection, also a word for the sun. In Punjabi and Urdu, meher is grace or blessing, and the name is common in Sikh and Muslim families.
From Sanskrit yuga, an age or era, the word for the four great ages of the world in Hindu tradition. Yug is the modern Hindi form.
From Dutch bruin, brown, the name of the bear in the medieval Reynard the Fox tales, which gave English bruin as a word for a bear. It is also a Dutch surname.

assoc.t: Boston Bruins NHL hockey team
UCLA Bruins college sports teams

e.etymology: A spelling of Winona, from Dakota winuna, firstborn daughter. Country singer Wynonna Judd, born Christina Ciminella, made this spelling famous.

assoc.t: Wynonna Judd, country music star
Wynonna Earp, supernatural Western TV heroine

e.etymology: A recent name from India, where it took off in the 2010s alongside Amaira and Samaira. It has no agreed source and is often linked to Amira, Arabic for princess.
A recent American name that follows the sound of Leia, Elia and Eliana. It has no established meaning of its own.
For girls, a short form of Katherine and other names starting with K, popular on its own in the mid-1900s. For boys it is the Sir Kay of Arthurian legend, from Welsh Cai, the Latin Caius.
namesakes: Kay Bailey Hutchison (former US senator from Texas)
Sir Kay (knight of King Arthur's Round Table)
Kay Adams (Michael Corleone's wife in The Godfather)

assoc.t: Kay Jewelers, national jewelry chain
kay, a clipped way of saying okay

e.etymology: An English surname meaning son of Will, the short form of William. It was a common American first name in the late 1800s.
namesakes: Willis Reed (Hall of Fame center for the Knicks)
Willis Carrier (inventor of modern air conditioning)

assoc.t: Willis Jackson, the big brother on Diff'rent Strokes
actor Bruce Willis
Willis Tower in Chicago, the former Sears Tower

e.note: Expect to hear the Diff'rent Strokes line What'chu talkin' 'bout, Willis?

e.etymology: A single-S spelling of Melissa, from Greek melissa, honeybee, the name of a nymph who cared for the infant Zeus. This spelling is standard in Turkish and common in Spanish.
An English surname that began as a nickname for a brave man, from Old French hardi, bold or daring. The Danish first name Hardy comes separately from Germanic names containing hard.

assoc.t: The Hardy Boys, teen detective book series
Laurel and Hardy, classic film comedy duo
HARDY, country singer and songwriter
hardy, the English word for tough and resilient
actor Tom Hardy

e.etymology: In Vietnamese, mai is the yellow apricot blossom of the New Year, from the Chinese word for plum. Mai is also a Japanese name, often written as dance, and a Scandinavian form of May and Maria.

assoc.t: mai tai, the rum cocktail
Mai, knife thrower in Avatar: The Last Airbender

e.etymology: A respelling of Kendall, an English surname from the town of Kendal in Cumbria, the valley (dale) of the River Kent. It has been a girls' name in the US since the 1990s.

assoc.t: Amazon Kindle e-reader, if read as KIN-dul

e.note: The y invites the reading KIN-dul, like Amazon's Kindle.

e.etymology: In Dutch, a short form of Roeland (Roland) and Roelof (Rudolf), both built on a Germanic word for fame. In the US it is used mostly in Mexican American families, where Roel is also a surname.
A modern American blend of Aubrey and Brianna or Anna. Aubrey comes from the Germanic name Alberich, elf ruler, by way of Norman French.
A surname with two sources: an Irish and Scottish form of Fergus, and the Norman name Ferrers, from Ferrieres in France, a place of ironworks (French fer, iron).

assoc.t: Ferris Bueller of Ferris Bueller's Day Off
Ferris wheel, the fairground ride

e.note: Nearly everyone will think of Ferris Bueller or the Ferris wheel.

e.etymology: The name of the chief Egyptian god Amun, from Egyptian imn, the hidden one. A separate Hebrew Amon, read as faithful, was a king of Judah in the Bible.
namesakes: Amon-Ra St. Brown (Detroit Lions wide receiver)
Amon Goeth (Nazi commandant portrayed in Schindler's List)

assoc.t: Amon-Ra, king of the gods in ancient Egypt
Amon, masked villain of The Legend of Korra

e.etymology: A respelling of Aaron, used for girls as a twist on Erin as well as for boys. Aaron is Hebrew Aharon, the brother of Moses; its meaning is not known for certain.
From an English surname, probably from an Old English personal name joining sael, prosperity, and wig, battle. As a first name it is most common in Honduras and Guatemala.
